sections.heading: How Our Roofing Contractors Perform Infrared Roof Leak Detection

runs.v: ASTM C1153 Scan in the Optimal Thermal Window

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing scans the roof to ASTM C1153 in the optimal thermal window, after sunset on a dry surface, because wet insulation cools more slowly than dry and releases its retained heat as a warm anomaly on the thermal image.

runs.v: Scans are typically performed at night after the roof has absorbed solar energy during the day, and infrared thermography requires specific environmental conditions to yield accurate results: no appreciable rain in the roughly 48 hours prior, a dry surface free of standing water, snow, and debris, wind under roughly 15 mph, and a temperature differential near 10°C, 18°F, per ASTM C1153 via IIBEC and Fluke.
Verification by Core Cut and Moisture Meter

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing verifies every thermal anomaly by core cut, probe, or calibrated moisture meter before it is reported as wet insulation.

runs.v: A thermal imager detects temperature differences indicating moisture presence, and modern imagers resolve about 0.2°F, but the wet-area contrast narrows to about 5°F in winter against 20°F in summer, per IIBEC and Fluke, so a winter scan carries more false positives that physical verification resolves.
Wet-Insulation Mapping and Entry-Detail Tracing

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing maps the verified wet-insulation extent and traces it back toward the flashing detail that admits the water.

runs.v: The thermal map locates the wet insulation, not the entry point, so a Newark Quality Roofing report pairs the wet-insulation boundary with the verified entry detail, per Fluke and IIBEC.

sections.heading: How Roofers Find Leaks: Infrared Roof Inspections vs. Electronic Leak Detection vs. Flood Testing

runs.v: How do roofers find leaks in the roof? They start with a visual inspection of the flashing, seams, drains, and penetrations, then pick a test to fit the roof type. Good roof leak detection services match the method to the roof, and on a low slope roof three methods do most of the work.
Infrared Inspection and Core Cut Verification

An infrared inspection answers where the roof is wet. It covers the whole roof in one pass and shows the extent of the damage, but it reads wet insulation rather than the hole, and every anomaly needs a core cut or moisture meter.
Electronic Leak Detection on a Commercial Roof

Electronic leak detection answers where the hole is. A low- or high-voltage current is applied across the roofing membrane and traced to the breach, as described in ASTM D7877, the guide to electronic leak location in waterproof membranes. It needs a conductive layer below the membrane and can work under ballast or a vegetated roof, but it does not show how much insulation is already wet.
Flood Testing on a Commercial Building

Flood testing answers whether an area holds water. A section of a flat roof or deck is dammed, flooded, and held while the space below is watched, as described in ASTM D5957, the guide to flood testing horizontal waterproofing. It suits new waterproofing and small areas; on an older commercial building, water at about 5.2 pounds per square foot per inch of depth makes a large flood test a structural question, and a failed test soaks the insulation.

sections.heading: What an Infrared Moisture Scan Cannot See

c.v: Can infrared technology detect roof leaks? It detects the wet insulation a leak leaves behind, which is invisible to the naked eye, not the leak itself.

runs.v: Can an infrared camera detect water leaks? Only indirectly: infrared cameras read temperature on exterior surfaces, never water, so a small, fresh leak can go undetected. Even advanced thermal imaging struggles here:

c.v: Ballast, pavers, or a vegetated roof

items.v: covered over the membrane even out the thermal pattern.

c.v: Closed-cell foam insulation

items.v: holds less water than fiberboard or perlite, so wet areas show weaker contrast.

c.v: Bare metal surfaces

items.v: reflect the sky, so readings are unreliable.

c.v: A steep-slope shingle roof over a vented attic

items.v: has no wet insulation against the roof surface to read.

c.v: The entry point itself

items.v: stays invisible, because water travels before it soaks the insulation.

runs.v: Rooftop equipment, patches, and changes in roof type can also mimic moisture, which is why every anomaly is verified.

faqs.q: How does infrared roof leak detection find a leak?

runs.v: It scans the roof after sunset and maps the wet insulation, which holds solar heat longer than dry insulation and shows as a warm anomaly; by day the same areas can look cooler.

faqs.q: Does infrared imaging find the exact leak entry point?

runs.v: No. Infrared imaging locates the wet insulation, not the entry point, because water travels through the roof assembly before it soaks in.

faqs.q: Why does ASTM C1153 require a core cut?

runs.v: ASTM C1153 requires every suspected wet area to be verified by core cut, probe, or calibrated moisture meter, because a thermal anomaly indicates suspected moisture rather than a diagnosis.

faqs.q: What conditions does an infrared roof scan need?

runs.v: A dry surface, no appreciable rain for roughly 48 hours, light wind, an adequate temperature differential, and a scan after sunset.

faqs.q: How much does infrared roof leak detection cost in Essex County, NJ?

runs.v: The cost depends on roof size, roof system, and verification scope. Newark Quality Roofing provides a free written estimate.

faqs.q: Can infrared roof leak detection scan any commercial membrane?

runs.v: It scans insulated low-slope membranes including EPDM, TPO, and modified bitumen; ballast, pavers, and vegetated covers reduce the thermal contrast.

faqs.q: How does infrared roof leak detection differ from a thermal imaging inspection?

runs.v: Infrared roof leak detection focuses on locating and verifying the wet insulation behind an active or suspected leak, while a roof thermal imaging inspection surveys the whole roof for moisture, insulation, and energy performance.
